passage:
Dear Karthik,
I'm writing because I owe you an apology. Last Thursday at the bus stop, you were upset about your result, and I flung both my arms open and tried to hug you. You stiffened and stepped back, and I saw your face change. I wanted to help, but I didn't ask. I've thought about it all week. Afterwards you said, "Not now, just sit with me," and we sat until the bus came. That was better. Next time I'll ask, "Do you want a hug, or should I just stay here?" and I'll take whichever answer you give. Thank you for telling me straight.
Asif

qa.q: Where were Asif and Karthik when Asif tried to hug Karthik?
qa.a: They were at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when flinging both arms open, and what does Asif feel now?
qa.a: Asif wanted to comfort Karthik at the time. Now Asif regrets not asking first and wants to make up for it.

qa.q: What could Asif do next time a friend is upset?
qa.a: Asif could ask if a friend wants a hug or just company, and accept the answer. A refusal should be respected.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Asif's arms opened?
qa.a: Karthik stiffened and stepped back, which suggests being caught off guard and not wanting a hug then. Karthik may still have valued Asif sitting beside Karthik.

grounding: A teenager opens their arms for a friend who is upset, then learns to ask first because consent applies to every hug.

passage: You asked about the time I got it wrong, so here it is. Wasim had just failed the school band audition, and he was standing by the lockers, eyes wet. I went straight in with my arms wide open. He put a hand up, not rudely, and said, "Not a hugger today, bro." I dropped my arms, felt a bit foolish, and said, "Fair. Chai instead?" He half-smiled. We walked to the canteen, and he told me everything over two cups. Since then I ask first: "Hug, or just company?" Sometimes the answer is hug. Sometimes it's chai. Either way, the friend chooses. I'm Suraj, by the way, and that's my rule.

qa.q: What did Wasim say when Suraj opened his arms?
qa.a: He said, "Not a hugger today, bro."

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling after Wasim put up a hand?
qa.a: He felt a bit foolish but accepted it and wanted to keep comforting in another way. His quick "Fair. Chai instead?" shows he wasn't offended.

qa.q: What could a friend do to comfort someone without pushing a hug?
qa.a: Ask, "Hug, or just company?" and offer another kind action such as chai. Then let the friend choose.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt about Suraj's response?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved that his no was respected, and comforted enough to talk. He half-smiled and told everything.

grounding: A teenager opens his arms for an upset friend, is refused, and learns to ask first, with the refusal respected.

passage:
After the student council results, I saw Reena's friend Sneha sitting on the steps behind the library, crying. She'd lost by six votes.
Reena sat down next to her, then opened her arms a little and asked, "Hug? Or not right now?"
Sneha shook her head. "Not right now."
Reena didn't look hurt. She just lowered her arms, stayed close, and passed Sneha a tissue. They sat there for a long time. Reena didn't say much, just "That really stinks," once.
After a while, Sneha leaned her head on Reena's shoulder by herself.
I don't know what Reena was thinking. But she didn't push, and it seemed to help.
- Anirban

qa.q: How many votes did Sneha lose by?
qa.a: Six votes.

qa.q: What might Reena have been feeling when Sneha said no to the hug?
qa.a: Reena may have felt a small pang, but she seemed calm and caring, accepting the answer and staying close; Anirban can't be sure what she thought.

qa.q: What did Reena do that respected Sneha?
qa.a: She asked before hugging, accepted the refusal without sulking, and offered comfort in another way by staying close and passing a tissue.

qa.q: How might Sneha have felt when Reena asked instead of just hugging?
qa.a: Sneha probably felt respected and safe, which may be why she leaned on Reena's shoulder later by her own choice.

grounding: An observer sees a teenager open her arms and ask before hugging an upset friend, and respect the refusal.

passage:
Monday: When Jasleen cried after her grandmother's hospital news, Naveen rushed over and hugged her tight without asking. Jasleen went stiff and pulled away. "Please don't."
Naveen stepped back, embarrassed.
Wednesday: Naveen thought about it. He'd wanted to help. But Jasleen's stiff body had said something clear.
He asked his sister what to do. She said, "Ask first. Every time. Even with friends."
Friday: Jasleen's grandmother was better, but Jasleen cried with relief at lunch. Naveen sat next to her and opened his arms slightly. "Want a hug?"
Jasleen paused, then nodded. "Yes, please."
This time the hug was short and warm, and she smiled after.

qa.q: What did Jasleen say when Naveen hugged her on Monday?
qa.a: "Please don't."

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Jasleen pulled away on Monday?
qa.a: Naveen felt embarrassed and a bit hurt, since he only wanted to help.

qa.q: What did Naveen change by Friday, and why was it better?
qa.a: He opened his arms and asked first, letting Jasleen choose, which respected her and made the hug feel warm instead of forced.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt when Naveen asked on Friday?
qa.a: Jasleen probably felt respected and safe, which made her happy to accept the hug.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager learns to open his arms and ask before hugging a friend, after an unasked hug was refused.

passage:
"Akash, you asked why I always say 'Hug?' before hugging your aunt. Let your Tenzin Uncle tell you.
When I was sixteen, my best friend Karma's dog died. I found him behind the monastery wall, crying. I rushed and threw my arms around him. He froze, then pushed me off, hard, and walked away.
I was so hurt. I only wanted to comfort him.
Two days later, he told me, 'I needed to cry alone first. You didn't ask.'
From then on, I ask. I open my arms and say, 'Hug?' If they say no, I sit nearby or bring tea. It's their body, their choice. Even with people I love."

qa.q: Where did Tenzin find Karma crying?
qa.a: Behind the monastery wall.

qa.q: What was young Tenzin feeling when Karma pushed him away?
qa.a: Tenzin felt hurt and confused, because he had only wanted to comfort his friend.

qa.q: What choice inside the story taught Tenzin to ask first?
qa.a: Karma's choice to explain two days later that he needed to cry alone first taught Tenzin that consent matters even in comfort.

qa.q: How might Karma have felt when Tenzin hugged him without asking?
qa.a: Karma probably felt overwhelmed and crowded, needing space to grieve alone first.

grounding: An uncle recalls hugging a friend without asking and learning that every hug needs consent and a refusal must be respected.

passage: Rain was hammering the tin shelter outside the coaching centre, and the bus was due in five minutes. Dilnaz came out with her mock result crumpled in her fist, eyes red. Vikas started to open his arms, then stopped halfway. With everyone crowded under the shelter and the rain so loud, he had to lean close to be heard. "Do you want a hug, or no?" Dilnaz shook her head and folded her arms tight. "Not here. Not now." "Okay." Vikas lowered his arms and tilted his umbrella so it covered her instead. "Want me to just stand here?" She nodded. They stood side by side, not touching, until the bus splashed up. On the bus she finally said, "Thanks for asking first." He shrugged. "It's your call, always."

qa.q: What was Dilnaz holding in her fist?
qa.a: Her crumpled mock result.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he stopped with his arms halfway open?
qa.a: He felt caring and wanted to comfort Dilnaz, but was unsure whether a hug would be welcome in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Vikas still comfort Dilnaz after she said no?
qa.a: He lowered his arms without fuss, tilted the umbrella over her, and offered simply to stand with her.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when Vikas asked first?
qa.a: Dilnaz likely felt respected and less exposed, free to say no and still be supported 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a teenager opening his arms to comfort an upset friend, asking first whether a hug is welcome, and respecting her refusal.
